articles.title: The August 11, 1999 Total Solar Eclipse As Seen in the Black Sea
articles.summary: This article recounts the author's experience observing the August 11, 1999 total solar eclipse from the MV Marco Polo cruise ship in the western Black Sea. The ship positioned itself precisely at the center-line location, joined by several other vessels, under perfectly clear skies and calm seas for optimal viewing of the millennium's last total solar eclipse.

articles.title: A Miracle Near Munich
articles.summary: The author recounts a 'miracle' experience during an eclipse event on the morning of August 11th in Einsbach, Germany. Despite a cliff-hanger lead-up, the sky was perfectly clear, reminiscent of previous successful eclipse observations in India and Australia, leading the author to express a belief in miracles.

articles.title: Centerline through Bucharest
articles.summary: Daniel Stefanescu expresses his long-standing anticipation for an upcoming lunar eclipse, an event he has been looking forward to for over three years. The eclipse's centerline is calculated to pass within a quarter mile south of his childhood home in Bucharest, Romania, making it a particularly personal and significant astronomical event for him.

articles.title: SJAA Activities Calendar
articles.summary: This document outlines the activity calendar for the San Jose Astronomical Association (SJAA) from October 1999 to January 2000. It details numerous star parties at locations such as Henry Coe, Fremont Peak, Houge Park, and Pinnacles, along with general meetings featuring guest speakers on astronomical topics. The calendar also includes social events like a Christmas potluck and practical notes like the end of Summer time.

articles.title: Bob Garfinkle on the Black Sea
articles.summary: This article recounts Bob Garfinkle's experience observing a total solar eclipse from the Marco Polo cruise ship in the Black Sea. He details the preparations, equipment used, and specific observations made during the eclipse, including temperature drops, the appearance of the corona and prominences, and visible planets. The author also mentions fellow presenters like astronaut Jay Apt and the calm sea conditions that aided viewing, concluding with post-eclipse travel and a look to future expeditions.

articles.title: Ernie Piini from Germany
articles.summary: Ernie Piini recounts his challenging yet ultimately successful experience observing a total solar eclipse in Altomunster, Germany, with the Amateur Astronomers Inc. group. Despite initial heavy rain and overcast skies, the weather cleared just in time for a brief, spectacular view of the eclipse, featuring Baily's Beads, a Diamond Ring, and prominent rosy red prominences. Piini details his photographic setup and observations, highlighting the beauty of the event before the sky clouded over again.

articles.title: Continued from page three
articles.summary: A church ceremony featured a unique parade including two busses and a donkey, which was transported by trailer. The donkey, adorned with traditional wedding candles, delighted all attendees. The narrative also briefly mentions taking side trips around an eclipse.

articles.title: This eclipse was a real beauty. Was it because we prayed so hard for the sky to clear?
articles.summary: The article recounts a family trip through Italy and Germany, highlighting visits to places like Milan's Duomo and Munich's Deutch Museum, particularly its Amateur Astronomy section. The main focus is on a miraculous eclipse event, where the sky cleared after prayers, allowing the author's brother and cousins to witness the beautiful celestial phenomenon, leaving a lasting memory.

articles.title: David North
articles.summary: This article outlines the significant meteor showers occurring in November 1999, primarily focusing on the Leonids, which were expected to be highly active around November 17/18 due to comet Temple-Tuttle's activity, with a potential for a meteor storm. It offers observing advice, including peak times and dates, and notes that the Taurids, associated with comet Encke, also have two slower, brighter peaks earlier in the month.

articles.title: Daniel Stefanescu in Bucharest
articles.summary: This article details the author's preparations and observations for a total solar eclipse in Bucharest, highlighting the widespread local excitement despite economic hardships and the scarcity of souvenirs. The author describes setting up extensive equipment on his apartment building's rooftop, including cameras, filters, and instruments for measuring temperature and wind, while also noting the presence of celebrities like Luciano Pavarotti in the city. The narrative focuses on the meticulous planning and challenges faced right before first contact, ensuring he was ready for the astronomical event.

articles.title: Stefanescu from Centerline
articles.summary: The article provides a vivid personal account of observing a total solar eclipse from Bucharest, Romania, detailing the sensory experiences, atmospheric changes, and visual phenomena such as Baily's Beads, the diamond ring, and the solar corona. Following the eclipse, the author attended a reception hosted by the U.S. Ambassador, where astronomers and NASA director Dan Goldin were present to discuss space missions. The experience combined detailed astronomical observation with cultural engagement and personal travel.

articles.title: Dave North
articles.summary: This article details upcoming lunar libration events in November, offering specific observing opportunities for features like Mare Anguis and Mare Orientale. It also reflects on the relative lack of amateur astronomers who can identify numerous named lunar features compared to deep-sky objects, and corrects a previous explanation of libration in latitude thanks to reader feedback. Finally, it promotes an upcoming speaker, Michael Light, who compiled an impressive book and exhibition of Apollo mission lunar photographs.

articles.title: Show and Tell 1999
articles.summary: The SJAA's "Show and Tell 1999" event was a memorable slide and equipment night, highlighted by Paul Graves' captivating presentation of the 1999 Solar Eclipse from Hungary, complete with musical accompaniment and breathtaking aerial views. Attendees also showcased various astronomical equipment, including digital camera setups, new telescopes like Orion's Nextstar and Rich Neushaefer's AP scope, and a detailed 3-D lunar model. The evening combined personal observing experiences with demonstrations of amateur astronomy technology.

articles.title: The Shallow Sky
articles.summary: This article highlights the rare Mercury transit on November 15th, providing viewing tips such as using a solar filter and high magnification due to limb darkening. It also offers a guide to observing other planets in November, noting Jupiter's recent opposition with targets like the Great Red Spot, and Saturn's upcoming opposition showcasing its tilted rings and Cassini's division. Brief mentions are made of Mars, Neptune, Uranus, Pluto, and Venus's visibility.

articles.title: Comet Comments For November 1999
articles.summary: This article provides updates on several comets for November 1999, including Comet LINEAR (1999 J3), Comet Lee, and the return of Periodic Comet Machholz 2. It also mentions new comets discovered by SOHO and other instruments, highlighting Comet 1999 S4 (LINEAR) as a potential naked-eye object by mid-next year. Additionally, it reports on the re-funding and re-establishment of the Southern Hemisphere Near-Earth Object (NEO) search, managed by Robert McNaught, following its shutdown in 1996.

articles.title: LUNAR PHASES:
articles.summary: This document provides a schedule of the four main lunar phases for a specific period, detailing the exact date and time (PST) for New Moon, First Quarter, Full Moon, and Last Quarter. It also includes the corresponding rise, transit, and set times for each of these significant lunar events.

articles.title: NEARER PLANETS: R. A. Dec.
articles.summary: This document provides an ephemeris, detailing astronomical data for several 'Nearer Planets' including Mercury, Venus, Mars, Jupiter, and Saturn, along with the Sun (SOL). For specific dates (7th, 17th, 27th), it lists each body's Right Ascension (R.A.), Declination (Dec.), rise, transit, and set times, as well as their magnitude and distance in Astronomical Units (A.U.). This information serves as a guide for tracking the positions and visibility of these celestial objects.

articles.title: Astronomical Twilight:
articles.summary: This document presents a concise table detailing the start and end times of astronomical twilight for several specific Julian Dates. It provides a brief schedule for when dark sky conditions begin and end.

articles.title: Sidereal Time:
articles.summary: This document provides specific astronomical timings, including sidereal time values for various dates and times, such as transit right ascension and local midnight. It also details the celestial conditions for the "Darkest Saturday Night" on November 6, 1999, listing sunset, twilight end, moonset, dawn begin, and total hours of darkness.

articles.title: Ephemerides
articles.summary: This document provides ephemerides for three comets: C/1999 H1 (Lee), 141P/Machholz 2, and 1999 J3 (LINEAR). For each comet, tables list daily celestial coordinates (Right Ascension and Declination), elongation, sky visibility (morning or evening), and estimated visual magnitude from October to December. This data is crucial for astronomers to locate and observe these comets.

articles.title: Elements
articles.summary: This document provides detailed orbital elements for three celestial objects: Lee, P/Machholz 2, and LINEAR (1999 J3), listing parameters such as perihelion date and distance, inclination, eccentricity, and orbital period. It serves as an ephemeris for these objects with data points from 1999, along with references to MPC circulars. The article also includes contact information for astronomer Don Machholz and a request for questions for a San Jose Astronomical Association (SJAA) mailbag column.

articles.title: Officers and Board of Directors
articles.summary: This document lists the current officers and members of the Board of Directors for an organization. It details their specific roles, including President, Vice President, Secretary, Treasurer, and Director, along with their respective contact phone numbers.

articles.title: Ephemeris Staff
articles.summary: This document lists the staff responsible for the 'Ephemeris' publication, including contact information for its editors, circulation managers, and printing services. It provides names and phone numbers for each role, offering a clear point of contact for different aspects of the publication's production.

articles.title: SJAA Loaner Scope Status
articles.summary: The San Jose Astronomical Association (SJAA) currently has all of its loaner telescopes available for members. Interested SJAA members can contact Mike Koop via email or phone to borrow a scope.

articles.title: Stored Scopes
articles.summary: The San Jose Astronomical Association (SJAA) maintains a program called "Stored Scopes" that offers telescopes for immediate loan to its members. These scopes are stored at various members' homes, and interested individuals can arrange for pickup through Mike Koop at SJAA events. The inventory currently includes models like a 4" Quantum S/C and a 7" f/9 Newt/Pipe Mount.

articles.title: Current Scope Loans
articles.summary: This document lists telescopes currently loaned out, providing details such as the scope number, description, borrower, and due date. It also informs interested individuals that they can be placed on a waiting list for a specific scope once it becomes available after its due date. The list includes various types of telescopes, such as Newtonians, Dobsons, Celestron S/C, refractors, and a solar scope.

articles.title: Extended Scope Loans
articles.summary: This document outlines an "Extended Scope Loans" program, listing telescopes whose loan periods have been prolonged. It details the process for interested members to borrow these scopes, which involves coordinating a transfer with the current borrower. A table provides specifics for each extended loan, including the telescope type, current borrower, and the new (or indefinite) due date, along with a request for contact information for one specific borrower.

articles.title: Periodical Publication Statement
articles.summary: The SJAA Ephemeris, the official newsletter of the San Jose Astronomical Association, is published monthly throughout the year, from January to December. The document also provides the mailing address for the San Jose Astronomical Association in Campbell, CA.

articles.title: Submit
articles.summary: This article provides instructions for members of the SJAA to submit articles for publication in the SJAA Ephemeris newsletter, directing them to an editor's email. Additionally, it details the process for subscribing to or unsubscribing from the SJAA Mailing List via a specific email address and simple text commands.

articles.title: San Jose Astronomical Association Membership Form
articles.summary: This document is a membership form for the San Jose Astronomical Association (SJAA), dated November 1999. It details options for new or renewing members, including regular ($15) and junior ($6) memberships, with an additional $30 option for a Sky & Telescope subscription. Applicants are instructed to make checks payable to SJAA and submit the form at a meeting or mail it to their P.O. Box in Campbell, CA.
